what.title: What is Marvel?
what.metaDescription: Comics, then a studio, then a rights split. That is why a watch order is hard.
what.intro: Marvel is three things that people use one word for: a comics publisher, a film studio, and a set of characters other studios still partly own. The last one is why a watch order is hard.
what.payoffHeading: This is why the order is hard
what.payoff: One story runs through six sets of rights. That is the whole problem, and it is why this site has six universes rather than one list.
what.ch1Body: Timely Comics, later Marvel. Decades of characters built to cross over. That habit is exactly what makes a screen order complicated later.
what.ch2Body: Near bankruptcy, Marvel licensed its best-known characters out. Spider-Man went to Sony. X-Men and Fantastic Four went to Fox. Blade, Daredevil, Ghost Rider and Punisher went elsewhere again.
what.ch3Body: Left with the characters nobody else wanted, Marvel financed Iron Man itself, and built a connected universe out of what remained.
what.ch4Title: Netflix builds a corner of it
what.ch4Body: Thirteen seasons of Daredevil, Jessica Jones, Luke Cage, Iron Fist and Punisher ran alongside the films for years before being folded back in.
what.ch5Body: X-Men and Fantastic Four come home. Sony keeps Spider-Man and lends him out. The map stops getting simpler and starts getting tangled.

rights.metaDescription: One story, seven sets of rights, thirty years. This is why a watch order is hard.
rights.heading: One story, seven sets of rights
rights.lede: Marvel sold its characters off to survive the nineties. Everything confusing about the order comes from that, and from getting them back one studio at a time.
rights.payoff: That is the whole problem, and it is why this site has seven universes rather than one list.

universes.metaDescription: The X-Men, the Fantastic Four, the Spider-Verse, Marvel television, the animation, and what came before — each in release or story order, as posters or on a timeline.
universes.heading: The other universes
universes.lede: Marvel is not one thing. The MCU has its own page; everything else is here, each with the same two orders and two views.
universes.spoilerBody: A post-credits scene is written to surprise you at the end of one film and pay off in the next. Sorting by when events happen puts several of them before the films they were made to sell. Release order does not do this, which is why it is the default.

bridge.all: Every title this site holds, in one order. {n} of them, across seven studios and {years} years.
bridge.mcu: The spine everything else connects to. Twenty-three films to the end of the Infinity Saga, then the Multiverse Saga. The One-Shots are in the catalogue, not in the order.
bridge.x-men: Fox held these until Disney bought the studio in 2019, and the timeline was rewritten mid-run. This is why Deadpool & Wolverine reaches back two decades.
bridge.fantastic-four: The same studio, an entirely separate thing. Three attempts before Marvel Studios got the rights back.
bridge.spider-verse: Sony has held the Spider-Man film rights since 1999. Three live-action eras and an animated one, and the reason No Way Home needs homework.
bridge.marvel-tv: A different company from Marvel Studios: ABC, Freeform and Hulu, under a different executive. Absorbed in 2019, and its canon status went with it. Watch these because they are good, not because the films need them.
bridge.legacy: Everything live-action Marvel licensed out before it started making its own — the 1944 serial, the television Hulk, Blade, the Raimi era's ancestors.
bridge.animation: Separate continuities that borrow the same characters, and occasionally get referenced back.
bridge.defenders: Netflix's thirteen seasons ran alongside the films for years and then were folded in. One continuous story with its own crossover, and Echo requires all of it.

stan-lee.name: Stan Lee
stan-lee.line: Co-created most of the characters on this site, at Marvel Comics, largely between 1961 and 1972.
stan-lee.about: He was writing filler for a company that was about to fold when he was told to make a superhero team to compete with the Justice League. He wrote the Fantastic Four as a family that argued, and then spent eleven years doing the same thing to every archetype he touched: a teenager who could not pay rent, a scientist afraid of himself, a billionaire with a heart condition. The idea that a superhero has an ordinary problem is his, and it is why any of this survived the sixties. He died in November 2018, aged 95.
stan-lee.created: Mostly with Jack Kirby and Steve Ditko, who drew them and shaped them at least as much — a credit Lee spent decades being argued with about, and one this page states rather than steps around.
stan-lee.extra: He appears in almost every Marvel Studios film from 2008 onward, and in several of the Fox and Sony ones. His last filmed cameo was in Avengers: Endgame; the animated Spider-Verse films kept finding ways to include him after he died.

kevin-feige.name: Kevin Feige
kevin-feige.line: Has run the films since 2007. He is the reason they connect to each other at all.
kevin-feige.about: He started as an assistant on the first X-Men film and was made president of Marvel Studios in 2007, a year before Iron Man. The decision that defines everything on this site is his: that these films would share one continuity, in public, with a schedule announced years ahead. Nobody had tried it at that scale, and every studio has been trying to copy it since.
kevin-feige.extra: Producer on the first films, president of Marvel Studios since 2007, and Chief Creative Officer of Marvel since 2019. The connective structure this whole site maps is his.
